result: 0 upstream-reportable findings; 4 flags, all four false
the_actual_finding: the HIGH-FIDELITY classifier admitted all four. The gates are correct about the IR they were handed; the LIFTER produced IR that does not match the harness, and the fidelity signal -- 'the lifter could not attribute some values' -- did not fire on any of them. A fidelity signal that misses four out of four is the defect, not the gates.
CORRECTION: The population figures first recorded here (214 high-fidelity, 4 flagged, 1.9%) were produced by a script that detected fidelity by GREPPING THE CLI OUTPUT for 'could not attribute'. Changing that message then made 130 harnesses appear to become high-fidelity and the flags appear to vanish -- a result manufactured entirely by the measuring script. The audit is re-run through the lifter's API below. The four triage verdicts stand; they came from reading the harnesses, not from the script.

triage.bluez/fuzz_gobex.c: FALSE POSITIVE - same shape: a local passed by address, which for an out-parameter is uninitialised BY DESIGN
triage.sentencepiece/trainer_fuzzer.cc: S2.UNKNOWN_PARAM, not triaged in this round

after_fidelity_fix.remaining_lifter_gap: A CALLER-DECLARED LOCAL PASSED BY ADDRESS IS NOT AN UNCREATED RESOURCE. This one shape produced the tdengine, lcms, yajl-ruby and bluez flags -- it is the single largest false-positive source left, and fixing it is the prerequisite for running this audit for findings rather than for calibration.

fidelity_fixes_made: a call in the body that never became an op now makes the lift untrusted
a use of the data or size parameter that was never bound now makes it untrusted
comparison guards (`if (size < 4)`) are excluded, because counting them rejected a correctly lifted branching harness -- fail closed, but not shut

final.reading: The gate bank, restricted to lifts it can be trusted on, finds NO defects in 38 production OSS-Fuzz harnesses. Both numbers matter: zero false positives is the calibration this project never had, and zero findings is the honest cost of only grading what we can read.
final.coverage_limit: 38 of 372 is 10%. The bottleneck is no longer the gates, it is how much of a real harness this lifter can read. Raising the high-fidelity rate is what would turn this from a calibration into a search.
defects_fixed_getting_here: fidelity could not see a call that was never lifted
fidelity could not see an input flow that was never bound
the flow count treated `if (size < 4)` guards as unfollowed flows
the flow count compared data-uses against data+size bindings, so a length binding masked an unbound input
S1 tested `storage == 'out'`, a value the IR never uses -- so the caller-declared slot exemption it documents had never once fired
a slot the harness declares was treated as a resource awaiting a create
marking those slots alive then made every ordinary out-parameter a DOUBLE_CREATE
`x.push_back(y)` was lifted as a call to a C function named push_back, and graded
final.SUPERSEDED: The '38 high-fidelity, 0 flags' line below was measured with a shadowed exclusion set: a second `_NOT_A_CALL` defined for the missed-call check overwrote the module's own, dropping malloc, free, calloc and friends from the exclusion the LIFTER uses, so housekeeping calls were lifted as library ops and changed what the gates saw. Corrected below.

triage.openvpn/fuzz_proxy.c: FALSE POSITIVE - S3.DESTROY_NO_TARGET on gc_free/free_buf. The harness frees correctly on every exit path (early return at lines 76-77, and again at 129-130). The tell is internal: op o18 resolves `gc_free(&gc)` to r_gc and op o5 does not resolve the IDENTICAL call. Same call, same argument, different answer -- a lifter that cannot resolve the target inside an early-return branch, not a defect in openvpn.

final_corrected.next_lifter_gap: resolve `&local` to its resource inside early-return branches; the same call resolves at the end of the body and not at the top.
final_corrected.process_note: THIS IS THE THIRD TIME TODAY THAT A CHANGE OF MINE MOVED THESE NUMBERS: a text-scraping fidelity detector, a DOUBLE_CREATE regression that took flags 3 -> 16, and now a shadowed set that took them 2 -> 0. Each was caught by a figure moving in a direction nothing justified. An audit is only as trustworthy as the last change to the thing doing the auditing, which is an argument for re-running it after every such change rather than reporting it once.

last_flag.why: `tmp` is assigned in MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE switch cases and freed in each (line 48). The lifter flattens the switch into a straight line, so two assignments on paths that never both run read as a create-then-create with the first leaked.

end_of_session.the_pattern: EVERY false positive found today traces to one thing: the lifter reads a flat statement list, and real harnesses branch. Calls in `if` conditions, frees on early-return paths, assignments in exclusive switch cases, input reaching a call through a struct initialiser or a global -- each was patched individually and each was the same root cause wearing different clothes. The flat model is the limitation, not the rules built on it.
end_of_session.conclusion: Two structural pieces of work stand between this audit and upstream findings, and neither is a patch: a C++ lifter (60% of the fleet, 7% readable) and control flow the lifter can actually follow. Until both exist, this audit is a calibration instrument -- which it now is, honestly: 0 findings, 1 false positive, 44 readable.

after_branch_arms.what_changed: The lifter now tracks WHICH ARM a statement is in, not just how deep it is nested, and a switch body is cut into one arm per case label. Two creates on paths that never both run are no longer a leak. That cleared the last flag -- openvpn's `tmp`, assigned in thirteen mutually exclusive cases and freed in each.
after_branch_arms.reading: Zero flags on 44 readable lifts of production harnesses. Every false positive this audit produced has now been traced to a cause and fixed, and the causes were all one thing: a flat statement model applied to branching code. Still zero findings -- the instrument is calibrated, and 44 of 372 is what it can currently read.

after_alias_taint.what_changed: The lifter now propagates taint through a plain assignment. `const uint8_t *payload = data; size_t payload_len = size;` was the most common shape it could not follow: both arguments bound as LITERALS and the harness read as consuming no input.
after_alias_taint.correction: THIS CORRECTS AN EARLIER CONCLUSION IN THIS FILE. The bottleneck was diagnosed as 'a C lifter cannot read C++ harnesses' on the strength of the .c/.cc readable split, and that was measured twice and stated confidently. It was partly wrong. The largest single category was plain ALIASING, which is not a C++ construct at all -- fixing it took .cc from 7% to 17% and .c from 19% to 22%. The split was real; the cause attributed to it was not. Reading five failing harnesses would have shown this in minutes, and counting them by extension did not.
after_alias_taint.still_true: C++ remains under-read relative to C, and a C++ lifter is still the larger structural piece. But it is now worth about 5 points of the gap rather than all of it.

end_of_session_final.session_arc: 44 readable -> 117 readable, 4 flags -> 0, across ~17 defects in the lifter and gates. No findings at any point.
end_of_session_final.the_diagnosis_that_was_wrong: C++ was identified as the ceiling, twice, from the readable split (.c 19% vs .cc 7%). C++ harnesses are now MORE readable than C ones -- 37% against 23% -- and not one of the fixes that got there was a C++ lifter. They were aliasing, copiers, casts, and two of our own checks disagreeing about the same exclusion set. The split was real and the inference from it was wrong.
end_of_session_final.method_that_worked: Reading failing harnesses. Every time the counts were aggregated by category the conclusion was wrong; every time five files were opened and read, the cause was obvious within minutes. A distribution says where to look, never what you are looking at.
end_of_session_final.still_zero_findings: 117 readable production harnesses, no defect found in any of them. That is the honest result: these are maintained harnesses that have been fuzzing for years, and the instrument is now calibrated at 0% false positives rather than 'untested at scale'.

why_zero_findings.question: QuartetFuzz found 53 protocol violations in 586 harnesses (~9%). We found 0 in 117. If their rate held we would expect ~10. Which is it: our gates check weaker things, or our fidelity filter excludes the defective ones?

gate_firing_census.note: counts are ALL 358 lifts / high-fidelity only

why_zero_findings.finding_1: EVERY BLOCKING VIOLATION OCCURS ONLY IN LOW-FIDELITY LIFTS. Zero in trusted ones. That is consistent with triage -- every blocking flag examined today was a lifter artifact -- but it also means the trusted set currently has no blocking violation of any kind, and a filter that selects for 'the lifter understood everything' may be selecting for 'nothing looks odd'. Worth watching; not yet demonstrated either way.
why_zero_findings.finding_2: The warning tier is NOT a pile of undiscovered findings. S1.LEAK fires on 67 of 117 trusted lifts, which looked like 67 candidate protocol violations sitting one tier below where anyone was looking. It is not. apache-httpd/fuzz_request.c calls af_gb_init() at line 65 and af_gb_cleanup() at line 139 -- a harness-local bulk allocator freed in one call. Our S1.LEAK models per-resource destroys and cannot see bulk cleanup, so every arena-allocated resource reads as leaked.
why_zero_findings.conclusion: The 0 findings is genuine rather than an artifact of tier classification. It is not evidence the gates are strong: it is consistent both with 117 clean production harnesses and with gates that cannot yet see the defect classes QuartetFuzz reports.
why_zero_findings.next: Model BULK CLEANUP (apr_pool_destroy, arena/talloc contexts, harness-local collectors like af_gb_cleanup) so S1.LEAK stops firing on 57% of trusted lifts. Until then the warning tier is unusable for triage, which is its own kind of silent failure: a signal so noisy nobody reads it.
